newsitem.title: UK: OLYMPICS-BRITISH BID TO BECOME WINNERS AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-BRITISH BID TO BECOME WINNERS AGAIN.

text.p: The race is on to transform British sportsmen into winners again, fired by Prime Minister John Major's 100 million pounds ($160 million) initiative.
He has promised that sum from the national lottery for an academy of sport, inviting bids from allcomers to get it started.
A group calling itself Central Consortium is hoping to set the pace and has promised greater sporting success for Britain if it wins.

The group is led by Sir Nigel Rudd, 49-year-old head of an international manufacturing conglomerate, and he is confident the establishment of the academy would quickly lead to an improvement in standards.
"When all sport was amateur, Britain did well enough. It has not coped with the professional era," he said.
"Because our bid includes substantial elements which are already established, or are on the starting blocks, it can be turned into action quickly and efficiently.
"As a result, we are uniquely able to pledge the nation more medals and more sporting successes at the 2000 Sydney Olympics."

British sports fans would certainly hope for better than Atlanta 1996. Fifteen medals but only one gold (won by rowers Steve Redgrave and Matthew Pinsent) left the team 36th in the table, having been a passable 13th four years previously.

Sir Nigel asserts: "Sporting excellence unites and inspires the nation, which is why we are launching our bid. The Prime Minister's vision is to give our sportsmen and women the support they need on the world stage. We will deliver that vision."

The wealthy businessman has a modest but enthusiastic sporting background himself. He was a junior county tennis player for Derbyshire and is a keen supporter of soccer, squash, rugby and athletics and is helping to launch the benefit season of England cricketer Devon Malcolm.
The academy's headquarters would be sited at Nottingham and would draw on, and improve, existing facilties in the English midlands.

They include: Loughborough University, which specialises in sport, its most famous student being double Olympic 1500 metres champion Sebastian Coe; Nottingham's rowing and canoeing courses, as well as its university sports medicine centre; and Lilleshall, which encompasses the Football Association's centre of excellence and a home to British gymnasts.

Sir Nigel said short-term improvement was possible because existing facilities would be used and the academy would be regionalised, unlike that in Canberra, Australia, which took 10 years to show results.

He adds: "We aim to be operational in September 1997 with full development in place by September 1999. The capital cost of the project will be about 158 million pounds ($252 million), of which 38 million pounds ($60 million) will come from the consortium. That not provided by the lottery will come from sponsorship and private sector investment."

Among his supporters are Coe, now a member of Parliament, England footballer Alan Shearer, British Lions rugby union manager Fran Cotton, and javelin thrower Steve Backley, winner of a silver medal at Atlanta and bronze at Barcelona in 1992.
There are expected to be about 20 bids to run the academy of sport, cut to a short list before the end of the year and with the winner declared in January.
